narrative: A 29-year-old Syrian Kurd left Irbil, Iraq, for Minsk in Belarus in late September 2021, part of the new wave of Syrians fleeing not the war itself but the misery of its aftermath - poverty, corruption and shattered infrastructure. From Belarus she set out to cross into the European Union on foot through the wet, dark forests of Poland toward Germany. She had already walked for 60 hours when she twisted her knee. It was not her first setback: earlier, her best friend and traveling companion had fainted in a panic attack as Polish border guards chased them, and they hid in ditches and behind trees while she tried to catch her breath; when they turned themselves in, the guards dumped them back across the border into Belarus. They returned, bedraggled and wet, on the same trail. After twisting her knee she persevered, dragging her injured leg behind her for two more days through rain and freezing temperatures, surviving on biscuits and water, the six of them sleeping sitting up on a single dry mat. Finally they reached a Polish village where a car took them across the border into Germany. She applied for asylum in the central German town of Giessen, saying she had put up with the unbearable pain because running away from something is sometimes the easiest thing, and that there was no future for her in Syria.
